data.content_ref: inline:The target's argument is circular at its load-bearing premise. It asserts that preferring Theory A over B 'is to assert that Theory A is more likely to yield successful outcomes,' then concludes that this smuggles in induction. But Popper's well-known concept of 'critical preference' is precisely a mode of action-guiding preference that does NOT assert higher probability — one chooses the better-tested theory because it has survived more severe criticism, while remaining open to refutation, without any claim that past success probabilistically predicts future success. The target even lists the defeating countercondition ('If one can define "rational action" without reference to expected utility or probability') but never argues why it fails. By assuming preference entails a probability claim (the very thing Popper denies) in order to prove that preference entails a probabilistic-inductive claim, the argument begs the question rather than mounting a case against Popper's actual position.
